note: When two JSON values mean the same setting. Both clients implement this and both run these cases. Numbers are the reason it is not plain structural equality: the native client parses with JSONSerialization, which compares NSNumbers numerically and re-emits them in its own spelling, so no client can keep a number's exact text. Measured against Foundation, not assumed.

cases.name: an integer and the same value written as a decimal
integers past the precision of a double are still told apart
a value that underflows a double is the value it underflows to
trailing zeroes do not make a different number
a number and its string spelling are different values
objects compare by content, whatever order they were written in
an object with an extra key is a different object
numbers nested in an array follow the same rule
numbers nested in an object follow the same rule
an empty object is not an empty array

knownDivergences.case: a boolean against the number it is represented by
knownDivergences.why: Foundation parses JSON `false` into an NSNumber, and NSNumber compares booleans against integers numerically, so the native client reads `false` and `0` as the same value. serde_json keeps them as distinct types. Both clients *store* them correctly — measured: a round trip through either writer leaves `false` as `false` and `0` as `0` — and both encode settings from typed models, so neither ever writes one where the other would write the other. Recorded rather than reconciled: making Rust agree would carry a Foundation representation quirk into a client that does not share it, to settle a case that cannot arise. Desktop's stricter reading is the safe direction — it writes when unsure rather than skipping a write it should have made.
